prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Biscuit, Crab, Trapezoid

outputs.L1:
At the stables, each stall bore a name. Biscuit stood aloof—I faced, always and invariably, his clockwork tail. Crab knew the salt lick too well. Trapezoid had mastered stillness: a midnight mare, she was the sternest and tallest, her chest stretched against the edges of her stall.

I was not afraid of Never, the chestnut gelding, and so rode his iron haunches as far as Panther Gap. Never and I lived in Virginia then. We could neither flee nor be kept. Seldom did I reach the little mountain without him, its easy crests making valleys of indifferent grasses.

What was that low sound I heard, alone with Never? A lone horse, a lodestar, a habit of fear. We think of a horse less as the history of one man and his sorrows than as the history of an entire evil time. Why I chose Never, I’ll never know.

I fed him odd lettuce, abundant bitterness. Who wore the bit and harness; who was the ready steed? Never took the carrot—words, by my own reckoning, an account of creeks and oystercatchers.

Our hoof-house rested at the foot of the mountain, upon which rested another house, more brazen than statuary. Let it be known: I first mistook gelding for gilding. I am the fool who has faith in Never. Somewhere, a gold door, burdened with apology, refuses all mint from the yard.
outputs.L2:
In the stable, every stall bore its occupant’s name. Biscuit kept his distance; whenever I looked at him, I was met by the mechanical sweep of his tail. Crab was overly familiar with the salt block. Trapezoid had perfected immobility. A black mare, she was the tallest and most severe, her chest pressing against the boundaries of her enclosure.

Never, the chestnut gelding, did not frighten me, so I rode atop his hard hindquarters all the way to Panther Gap. At that time, Never and I lived in Virginia. Escape was impossible for us, yet neither could we be confined. I rarely arrived at the small mountain without him, where gentle ridges turned stretches of unremarkable grass into valleys.

What was the faint noise I heard when Never and I were by ourselves? One solitary horse, a guiding star, a fear grown customary. We regard a horse not so much as the record of a single man and his grief as the chronicle of an entire wicked age. I cannot say why I selected Never. I gave him strange lettuce, bitterness in plentiful supply. Which of us carried the bit and bridle, and which stood prepared to be ridden?

Never accepted the carrot—and, as I calculated them, the words too: a tally of streams and oystercatchers. Our hoofed dwelling stood at the mountain’s base; upon the mountain sat a second house, more audacious than any statue.

This should be recorded: at first, I confused *gelding* with *gilding*. I am the fool who places trust in Never. Somewhere, a golden door weighed down by remorse rejects every bit of mint offered from the yard.
outputs.L3:
Each horse in the stable possesses a distinct and memorable identity. Biscuit is aloof and distant, Crab has an odd fondness for salt, and Trapezoid is stern and towering, commanding attention through sheer size and temperament. Among these sharply drawn animals, the narrator chooses to ride Never, a chestnut gelding, through the Virginia landscape as far as Panther Gap.

The relationship between the narrator and Never is both intimate and uneasy. They seem inseparable, yet their bond is shaped less by simple affection than by loneliness, habit, and fear. Their dependence on one another carries an undercurrent of discomfort, as though neither can fully escape the pain that holds them together. As the journey continues, Never comes to represent more than the narrator’s private sorrow. He becomes a symbol of a wider history—the enduring damage and moral burden left by an evil time.

Even so, the narrator does not abandon him. Despite bitterness, confusion, and faith placed where it may not belong, the narrator continues to trust Never and care for him. That loyalty is neither uncomplicated nor sentimental; it persists in full awareness of suffering and uncertainty. In this way, the bond between rider and horse becomes an act of endurance, revealing how care can survive even when trust has been wounded and the past remains impossible to escape.
outputs.L4:
Fear entered the stable before I did. It waited in the dark between the stalls, in the restless stamp of a hoof and the small metallic shaking of a bit against a tooth. Sorrow lived there too, though more quietly. It gathered in the worn halters, in the blankets folded for horses that would not need them again, and in the names painted above empty doors.

There had been many horses. Mercy, a gray mare who distrusted every open hand. Gabriel, tall and black, who carried himself like a messenger who had forgotten the news. Little Sunday, patient with children and merciless toward dogs. Their names had seemed half prayer, half command, as if naming an animal might bind its nature or persuade Providence to take notice.

Then there was Never.

Never was a chestnut gelding with a narrow white blaze and one dark hoof. In summer his coat shone like copper; in winter it roughened to the color of old leaves. He was not the fastest horse in the stable, nor the strongest, nor the easiest to ride. He hated low roofs, sudden ropes, and men who approached him from behind. At a gate he would pause as though the opening were another kind of wall. Yet once he chose a road, he went forward with a grave determination that made every mile feel necessary.

I rode him through Virginia in a season when the country itself seemed unable to decide whether it was opening or closing. The roads passed between split-rail fences, over ridges blue with distance, and down into valleys where mist covered the fields until the barns appeared to float. We crossed creeks swollen by rain and followed old turnpikes through towns whose courthouse statues faced one century while the shop windows advertised another. Everywhere there were signs of possession: stone boundaries, posted woods, locked sheds, pasture gates chained twice.

From the saddle, the land looked spacious. From the road, it seemed divided into a thousand enclosures.

Never felt each boundary before I saw it. His ears tilted toward wire hidden in weeds. He shortened his stride near narrow bridges. When a truck approached, he gathered himself beneath me, ready either to bolt or to fight an enemy made only of noise. I would tighten the reins, speaking his name as if it were a prohibition.

“Never. Easy, Never.”

The word sounded strange in my mouth. It could mean refusal, warning, or eternity. Sometimes I wondered whether the people who named him had intended a joke. More often I thought they had stumbled upon the truth: that every creature carries some final country into which no rider can follow.

We argued constantly. At crossroads he wanted the shaded lane, while I insisted on the paved road. At water he would stop and stare at his own broken reflection. I pressed my heels against his sides; he resisted the bit. I called it training. He may have called it captivity. Yet when thunder moved over the mountains and the first hard drops struck the dust, he trusted my hands enough to run where I turned him. When I was tired or lost, I trusted the steadiness of his body beneath me.

That was the confusion at the heart of our bond. I controlled him, but I depended on him. He carried me freely only because leather, iron, fences, and habit had taught him the cost of refusal. Still, there were moments when obedience became something else—not surrender, exactly, but agreement. We moved together across the open ground, and neither command nor resistance passed between us. His stride lifted me beyond fear. For a few minutes, freedom seemed not to mean the absence of restraint, but the discovery of a rhythm larger than either of us.

I wanted to believe those moments were proof of love.

Faith often begins in such wanting. We see trust where there may only be exhaustion, grace where there may only be necessity. We make symbols of animals because they cannot correct us. Yet Never did correct me, in his fashion. He shied from shadows I dismissed and endured dangers I had exaggerated. He taught me that fear is not cowardice but knowledge carried in the body. He taught me that sorrow can become a discipline: one keeps walking, one accepts the weight, one crosses what can be crossed.

Years later, what I remember most is not any single journey but the sound of his hooves on Virginia roads. The rhythm changes with the ground—hollow on bridges, muffled in red mud, sharp against frozen ruts. Behind that sound lies the unrest of the time: old loyalties defended, new freedoms promised, violence disguised as order, and every public argument echoed privately in barns, kitchens, schools, and churches. We spoke of liberty while fastening buckles. We spoke of peace while gripping the reins.

Never’s story belongs to that contradiction. He was confined and powerful, obedient and unconquered. I loved him and used him. He trusted me and feared what my hands could do. Together we traveled through a landscape beautiful enough to invite faith and burdened enough to defeat easy belief.

When I think of him now, I see him standing at a gate in the early morning. Beyond him, the fields rise toward the mountains. The latch is open, but he does not move. I cannot tell whether he is waiting for permission, gathering courage, or simply listening to something beyond my hearing.

Then he steps forward.

For a moment I believe he has chosen me. For another, I believe he has chosen the road. And perhaps the truth—the truth of horses, of nations, of every troubled age—is that no one watching from behind can ever be certain.
outputs.L5:
At low tide, a small crab discovered a biscuit resting on a trapezoid-shaped rock. He circled it cautiously, tapping the golden edge with one claw.

“A strange shell,” he decided, “but an excellent-smelling one.”

The crab broke off a crumb and tasted it. Delighted, he carried the biscuit home piece by piece. By sunset, the trapezoid rock was bare, and the crab’s pantry was full—proof that even the sea can offer unexpected treasures.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about a narrator in Virginia riding a chestnut gelding named Never, blending horses, memory, fear, and historical sorrow.
counterfactuals.output:
In Virginia, I ride a chestnut gelding named Never, though every mile he carries me is already behind us. His mane smells of rain, iron, and the dark cupboard where my grandmother kept letters from men who did not return. Beneath his hooves, the red earth opens and closes like a mouth rehearsing names.

Never is afraid of white stones, black water, and the sudden flight of hats. I am afraid of what remembers us. Along the road, split-rail fences lean toward the fields as if listening. The fields have heard everything: harness bells, auction blocks, cannon fire, the whisper of bare feet seeking north beneath a sky that would not answer. Even now, wheat bends in the shape of vanished bodies.

At dusk, Never’s shadow becomes a regiment. It crosses the pasture without drums, each soldier carrying a photograph of someone else’s child. I pull the reins, but memory has no bridle. We pass a house with thirteen windows, all lit from within by a blue, underwater flame. In every window, my own face is older. In every room, a woman folds a bloodstained map and calls it a tablecloth.

Never steps carefully over a creek. The water runs backward, toward mountains purple as bruises. For one instant I see the dead kneeling there—not only the uniformed dead, but those whose names were entered as numbers, those driven from orchards and rivers, those buried beyond the church wall where the grass grows taller from shame. They lift their hands, and the water passes through them.

I press my cheek to Never’s warm neck. His heart is a locked room where thunder keeps pacing. Mine answers from far away.

Night comes down in pieces: a crow’s wing, a burned letter, a handful of cavalry buttons. Fireflies rise from the ditches, carrying their small, impossible lanterns. Never shies, then stands trembling. Together we watch the lights drift over Virginia, over the wounded hills, over the roads that insist on going somewhere.

“Home,” I tell him.

Never turns his chestnut head, his dark eye holding the whole ruined century.

Then we ride on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental literary passage set around a stable and mountain, featuring horses named Biscuit, Crab, Trapezoid, and Never. Use dreamlike imagery, wordplay, and fragmented narration.
counterfactuals.output:
At the foot of the mountain, the stable slept standing up.

Its roof wore snow like a second, quieter roof. Its doors breathed in their hinges. Inside: hay, leather, the damp alphabet of animals.

Biscuit dreamed of ovens.

Crab walked sideways through every memory, even those with narrow gates.

Trapezoid had four opinions about the moon, none parallel.

And Never—

Never was not there, exactly. Never was always arriving.

*

Morning fractured against the mountain.

A bell rang in the fog, or the fog rang inside the bell. The groom—whose name had been misplaced—counted the horses:

One, two, three, not.

Again:

Biscuit. Crab. Trapezoid. Ne—

The stable swallowed the syllable.

Outside, avalanches rehearsed their white applause. Inside, Biscuit chewed sunlight into smaller and smaller pieces. Crab watched the walls sidle past. Trapezoid stood at an impossible angle, geometrically homesick.

A horseshoe hung above the door, catching no luck at all.

*

At dusk, the mountain came down to drink from the trough.

It lowered its granite muzzle. Pines trembled along its neck. Snow loosened from its mane and became moths, or ashes, or tiny unfinished letters addressed to no one.

Never stepped from the last stall.

Black horse, blue shadow. Hooves full of midnight. Eyes like two doors opening inward.

“Where have you been?” asked the nameless groom.

Never answered by galloping without moving.

The stable lengthened. Each stall opened into another stable, another mountain, another weather. Biscuit became crumbs beneath a star’s tongue. Crab backed into tomorrow. Trapezoid unfolded—triangle, doorway, field.

And Never ran.

Never ran until the word wore out.

*

By morning there were four horses in the snow and no stable.

Or four stables and one horse.

Or only the mountain, dreaming it had hands, dreaming those hands smelled of hay, dreaming it could name what would leave it:

Biscuit.

Crab.

Trapezoid.

Never.

Never, never—

which is also the sound of hooves disappearing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, uncanny monologue in the style of modernist Southern Gothic fiction. Center it on a rider’s troubled bond with a horse named Never and include Panther Gap, a gold door, and the confusion of “gelding” with “gilding.”
counterfactuals.output:
I named him Never because every promise I made on his back came loose before sundown. Never again the bottle, I said; never again my brother’s wife; never again that road through Panther Gap where the laurel grows black under the limestone and the whippoorwill calls like a child shut in a well. The horse would turn one dark ear to me, hearing the lie while it was still warm in my mouth.

He was a red horse once, though age and weather scoured him to the color of old blood. My father bought him from a man with no left thumb, a traveling man who claimed the animal had been gelded late and therefore remembered too much. But I was ten and mistook gelding for gilding. For years I believed there was gold inside him, some thin holy leaf hammered beneath the hide, and that if I rode him hard enough the sweat would wash the plain horse away and show the treasure.

That is the trouble with words: they breed in the dark and foal monsters.

Never hated Panther Gap. At its mouth he would stiffen until I could feel his fear passing through the saddle into my bones, and I would mistake it for my own courage. I spurred him because my father had taught me that whatever trembles must be mastered, though he himself trembled every Sunday before the gold door.

You know the door I mean.

It stood alone in the woods above the Gap, fixed upright in a frame of cedar, with no wall on either side and no house behind it. Gold, or painted gold, or gilded—there is that word again, shining over the wound of another word. My father used to kneel before it. Sometimes he knocked. Sometimes something knocked back. When I asked what was beyond it, he said, What is always beyond a door, boy? And when I answered A room, he struck me for foolishness.

The last time I rode Never there, the day was hot enough to soften the tar on the county road, but beneath the trees our breath smoked. He went lame without limping. That is the only way to say it. Each step arrived broken, though every leg was sound. I told him forward. I told him I was master. I told him a number of things men tell animals when they cannot command themselves.

At the gold door he stopped.

It was open.

Beyond it lay not forest, though the forest continued plainly around it. Beyond it was my father’s stable as it had been before the fire: clean hay, bright harness, the blue coat of evening hanging from every nail. My father stood in the stall with his back to me, brushing a horse I knew was Never and knew could not be, because Never was beneath me, shaking so hard my teeth rang.

Then my father turned. His face had the long sorrowful muzzle of a horse. On his forehead a white star. In his hand he held the little crescent knife the traveling man had used, and he said, Come see what we cut away to make a creature gentle.

Never reared.

I went backward into the leaves, but he went forward through the door. Horse, saddle, bridle—all passed into that impossible stable, and the door swung shut with a sound like a shovel striking stone.

I beat upon it until the gold came off on my fists. Not gold. Paint. Beneath it, black wood. Beneath the black wood, another thin brightness. Gilding, gelding—I could no longer keep the words apart. One meant beauty laid over ruin. The other meant ruin laid under obedience. Perhaps there was never much difference.

At dusk the door opened again. Never came out alone.

He stood over me without reins or saddle. His eyes were changed. Not human—God spare him that—but knowing in the old animal way, which is deeper and has no mercy in it. I reached for his mane. He lowered his head, and for one breath I thought he meant to forgive me.

Then he spoke my name in my father’s voice.

I have ridden him ever since.

Do not ask where. A man may ride for thirty years and remain at the same gold door. A horse may carry him across Panther Gap and never move one hoof. Each night I say, Never again. Each morning he is saddled. And under his worn red hide something shines, not treasure, not holiness, but the keen edge of what was taken from us both—him to make him gentle, me to make me a man.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a paragraph of poetic prose in which stable life becomes an allegory for captivity, evil, and faith. Make the language strange and aphoristic, with rhetorical questions and recurring references to “Never.”
counterfactuals.output: In the stable, every kindness wears a halter. The hay is sweet, the water bright, the walls built against wolves—yet what is evil if not safety that has forgotten the sky? Never, says the iron latch. Never, answers the horse, though its blood still remembers distances. Who can distinguish shelter from a patient cage, or obedience from despair taught to kneel? The lantern burns like a small, bribed sun; the groom whispers mercy while tightening the strap. Never is the first commandment of captivity, but also the black seed of faith: Never believe the door is the world. Never mistake the hand that feeds you for the hand of God. Beyond the rafters, night gallops without a rider, and the soul, hearing it, stamps once in the straw.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an absurdist horse story using unusual sentence constructions and ominous symbolism. Include named stalls, a midnight mare called Trapezoid, odd lettuce, creeks, oystercatchers, and a mysterious house on a mountain.
counterfactuals.output:
At the north end of the stable stood seven stalls, though the stable had been built for six.

Their names, painted in white along the doors, were **MERCY**, **THIMBLE**, **THE EMPEROR’S WEATHER**, **SALT**, **MAYBE**, **NO**, and **AFTERWARD**.

Nobody admitted to naming them.

In AFTERWARD lived Trapezoid, the midnight mare.

Midnight not merely in color was she, but in behavior. Clocks slowed when she drank. Lanterns, brought near her, remembered being darkness. Her mane contained a silence so complete that moths fell out of it, asleep or dead or reconsidering.

Each morning, the stable boy Otho fed the horses hay, oats, and one leaf of odd lettuce.

The lettuce arrived every Tuesday in a locked violin case. It was purple at the stem, silver at the edges, and warm as a recently spoken lie. Sometimes the leaves bore small typographical marks—commas, mostly, though once Otho found an ampersand that bit him.

“Eat around the punctuation,” advised the veterinarian.

The veterinarian was an umbrella with spectacles, so Otho did not entirely trust him.

Beyond the stable ran three creeks. One ran east, one ran west, and the third ran upward, climbing the air in nervous loops toward a mountain. Along their banks gathered oystercatchers, grave in their black-and-white coats, their orange beaks pointed like accusations.

They did not catch oysters.

They caught names.

“Bernard,” cried one, snatching the name from a passing milkmaid.

“Wednesday,” cried another, pulling the day straight out of the calendar.

The milkmaid went home nameless. Wednesday never occurred again.

High above, on the mountain where the upward creek disappeared into cloud, waited a house.

A narrow house. A patient house. A house with thirteen chimneys and no visible door.

By day, it seemed very far away.

By night, it stood just behind the stable.

No one discussed this, except the horses, and the horses discussed it backward.

*Mountain the on house the from comes spoon the,* whispered the gelding in SALT.

*Door a becomes moon the when run,* replied the pony in MAYBE.

Trapezoid said nothing.

Then, on the last midnight of a month that had forgotten its own name, every stall door opened inward, though there was no inward left. Otho woke beneath a rain of horseshoes. The oystercatchers lined the rafters, each holding a stolen word.

“Blood,” announced one.

“Key,” announced another.

“Lettuce,” said a third, and looked embarrassed.

Trapezoid stepped out of AFTERWARD.

Where her hooves touched the floor, small creeks began. They hurried over the boards, climbed the walls, and flowed through the roof toward the waiting mountain. In each creek swam a tiny version of the mysterious house, windows lit, chimneys smoking.

Otho seized the violin case.

Inside lay one final lettuce leaf, black-veined and shaped like a hand. Across its surface, in dew, was written:

**FEED THIS TO THE HOUSE BEFORE IT LEARNS TO GALLOP.**

Too late, said the mountain, by moving slightly closer.

The house bent its knees.

Thirteen chimneys whinnied.

Then down the upward creek Trapezoid ran—or fell, depending upon which direction one believed. Behind her came Otho, clutching the ominous lettuce. Behind Otho came the oystercatchers, dropping names like coins. Behind the birds came all seven stalls, dragging the stable with them.

MERCY stumbled.

NO refused.

THE EMPEROR’S WEATHER rained from inside.

At the summit, the house opened a door it had not previously possessed. Beyond it was the stable, but older. In every stall stood Trapezoid, seven midnight mares gazing out with one shared eye.

“Which mouth?” Otho asked.

The house lowered its many roofs.

“All houses are mouths,” replied the umbrella veterinarian, who had been waiting there for centuries.

Otho fed the lettuce to the smallest window.

The mountain shuddered. The creeks stopped midair. The oystercatchers released every stolen name at once, and the sky became crowded with Bernards, Wednesdays, keys, blood, and several obsolete kings.

The house chewed.

The house swallowed.

The house became a horse.

Not a handsome horse. A horse of staircases and wallpaper, galloping on four long corridors, windows blinking along its flanks. It leapt from the mountain and vanished into the night, carrying every room with it.

All but one.

That room remains at the summit, doorless and warm.

Inside is a stall named **BEFORE**.

Inside the stall is one leaf of ordinary lettuce.

And each midnight, Trapezoid climbs the downward creek to stare at it, trembling—not with hunger, but with recognition.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
